metadata.title: Teaching strategies influencing learning strategies: Exploration of teaching and learning practices in a higher education context in Pakistan

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses a qualitative exploratory case study design in a single higher education institute in Northern Sindh, Pakistan, based on semi-structured group interviews and classroom observations (12 student-teachers and 2 teachers). The manuscript does not describe any use of ILSA-style sampling weights, replicate weights, or complex survey design adjustments, and it does not report any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or weighted estimation procedures. Because the analysis is thematic (Braun & Clarke) rather than a quantitative achievement-score modeling pipeline, survey-weight guidance for PV-based achievement estimation is not applicable here. Accordingly, no weight variable name can be extracted, and the findings should be interpreted as context-specific qualitative evidence rather than population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This study does not analyze cognitive achievement outcomes from ILSA/PISA-style scales with Plausible Values; instead, it uses qualitative thematic analysis of interview and observation data about teaching and learning strategies. Because there is no PV-based dependent variable, PV handling is not applicable. The paper also does not describe a quantitative missing-data procedure (e.g., imputation or deletion rules) because the core analysis is interpretive coding of transcripts and field notes rather than statistical modeling of numeric outcomes.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study was conducted in the Department of Education of a higher education institute in Northern Sindh, Pakistan. Participants were 12 student-teachers enrolled in the second year of the BEd (Hons.) program; from around 45 students who expressed willingness, 18 volunteered, and the 12 who responded first were selected as final participants due to manageability and time constraints. Two teachers teaching English to this cohort were also invited to facilitate observations. Data collection used semi-structured group interviews (two groups of six students; each interviewed once for 30–40 minutes, with some follow-up for clarification) and five semi-structured classroom observations; interview transcripts and observation field notes were coded using thematic analysis.

Data were collected through semi-structured group interviews with 12 second-year BEd (Hons.) student-teachers (two groups of six) and supported by five semi-structured classroom observations involving two English teachers. The analysis used thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke) to identify dominant teaching strategies (e.g., group work/discussions, practical work, repetition, questioning) and corresponding learning strategies (e.g., note-taking, discussion for theoretical subjects, metacognitive adaptation from cramming to deeper understanding). No machine learning models, predictive metrics, or PV-based achievement outcomes are reported, and therefore no accuracy/RMSE/AUC-type performance can be extracted. The authors also note limitations in generalizability due to the small, single-institute sample and the reliance on a limited number of observations. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: The manuscript is not an empirical large-scale assessment (ILSA/PISA) quantitative study and does not train or evaluate any machine learning models. It reports qualitative thematic findings from interviews and observations, so fields related to PV handling, missing-data handling for numeric modeling, survey-weighting, and ML performance metrics are not applicable or not reported.
